title: The Rock That Wouldn't Sink

topics.value_lesson: Slowing down and looking closely: the mystery is solved by patient observation, not luck.

spine: A floating stone on a black-sand beach leads a young storyteller and a rock-collecting friend to read the holes, colour, and weight of volcanic rocks as the lava's own handwriting.

child_name.role: The storyteller's childhood self in the tale — the name Nina calls across the beach

rock_name.role: The nickname Nina gives the floating pumice, used playfully through the story and written on its egg-carton label at the end

segments.text:
On my windowsill there is a row of stones, and every one of them is a story. There is a flat grey skipping stone, a pebble with a stripe clean around its middle, and at the end, in its own egg-carton box, a pale rock so light it feels like a trick. That one is called {rock_name}. Here is how it got its name.

I was nine that summer, and I spent it on a black-sand beach with Nina, who collected rocks the way other people collect stickers, and her dog Biscuit, who collected sticks the way other people collect absolutely everything. Biscuit charged driftwood. Biscuit charged seaweed. Biscuit charged his own shadow once, and won.

The sand was black because the whole beach was old volcano, Nina told me, crushed up fine as pepper.

We were squatting at a rock pool, dropping pebbles in. Plip. Plip. Every single one went straight to the bottom, the way rocks do. Then Biscuit came galloping up with a pale stone in his mouth, dropped it at my feet, and nose-bopped it into the pool. Bonk.

It bobbed.

It sat on top of the water like a cork in a bath, and Biscuit barked at it, and it bobbed some more.

"No," said Nina, in the voice she saved for excellent things. "Rocks sink. Everybody knows rocks sink. {child_name}, why is that rock floating?"

"Closely," I said. "Really, really closely."

Nina marched us down the beach to the family with the windbreak and the big umbrella, the ones who always had everything. She came back holding a magnifying glass the size of a dinner plate.

"Borrowed," she said, and flopped down on the sand. "Look."

I held the glass over the pale stone. And we both went very quiet.

It was covered in holes. Hundreds of them. Tiny pinprick holes, so small you could not fit a crumb in one, squashed up against each other until the whole rock looked like a sponge that had turned to stone.

"Bubbles," Nina breathed. "Somebody put bubbles in a rock."

I rubbed it with my thumb. It was scratchy, like a stiff dry sponge, the kind that scrapes the porridge pot. Scratch, scratch.

Biscuit wanted a look too. He shoved his nose right up against the holes, sniffed hard, and sneezed so violently he blew the rock clean off my knee. Then he sneezed again. Then he sneezed at his own sneeze, and we laughed so much we had to lie down on the peppery sand.

When we sat up, Nina opened her notebook and wrote, in big letters: CLUE ONE. HOLES.

"A rock full of holes would be light," she said slowly. "Like a sponge. Like bread." She tapped her pencil. "But {child_name}. Holes mean bubbles. And bubbles mean air. How does air get inside a hot melted rock?"

Biscuit sneezed at the rock again, as if to say, exactly.

"Weigh it," I said. "Properly. With numbers."

Nina's eyes went round with delight, because Nina brings a kitchen scale everywhere. To the beach. To birthdays. Once, famously, to the dentist. She dug it out of the picnic basket from under the sandwiches and set it on a flat rock like a scientist in a film.

"First, a normal rock," she said.

She picked up a black pebble, the same size as our floater, and plopped it on the scale. The numbers spun and settled.

"Now the mystery."

She lifted the pebble off and put the pale stone on. We leaned in. The numbers wobbled, thought about it, and stopped.

"Half," Nina whispered. "{child_name}, it's barely half the weight. A rock this big should feel like a potato, and it feels like a bread roll."

Biscuit decided this was his moment to help. He put one paw firmly on the scale, and the numbers shot up and went wild, and he looked at us as if to say, you're welcome.

"Biscuit. Off."

Off he got, extremely pleased with himself.

Nina opened her notebook and wrote, in big letters: CLUE ONE. LIGHT. Suspiciously light.

She underlined suspiciously three times.

"So it's true," she said. "It's not a trick. It's really, properly light." She tapped her pencil, frowning. "But that doesn't tell us why. Rocks don't go on diets. Something made this one light, and I want to know what."

Biscuit, who had been watching all this with his head on one side, decided that science was taking far too long. He trotted to a bare patch of sand and began to dig. Sand flew. Sand fountained. Biscuit dug like a tiny furry excavator with somewhere important to be, and Nina and I leaned in, because when Biscuit dug, he usually found something, even if it was only a bigger hole.

"Woof," said Biscuit, in the voice he saved for excellent things.

There, at the bottom of the hole, sat a second stone. Nina lifted it out and whistled. It was black as the inside of a pocket, glassy and cold, without a single hole in it, and so shiny I could see my own face in it, all smudged and wobbly, like a reflection in a spoon.

"No holes," Nina said. "Not one. Feel how heavy."

She was right. It sat in my hand like it meant it. Nina took the pale rock in her other hand and held both arms out like a balance scale. Up went one side, down went the other. Up, down. Up, down.

"Same beach," she said slowly. "Total opposites. One floats and fizzes with holes. One's a lump of black glass."

"What did you two find over there?" called a voice. Ranger Jo, who led the lava-flow walk, came crunching across the sand in her big boots. She crouched, turned the black stone over, tapped the pale one with a fingernail, and grinned the way grown-ups grin when they know something delicious.

"Well, well," she said. "Obsidian and pumice. Here's the funny part, rock hunters. These two came from the very same eruption. Same volcano. Same blast of lava."

Nina's mouth fell open. Mine too. Biscuit barked at both rocks, just to be thorough.

"But they disagree about everything," Nina said. "How can one eruption make two rocks that don't even act like cousins?"

"Up," said Nina. "Definitely up. I want to stand where it happened."

Ranger Jo led us up the cinder path, which crunched under our boots like breakfast cereal. Biscuit charged every switchback. "Firm trail here," said Ranger Jo, tapping it with her boot. "Step where I step."

At the top, she stopped. "Now then. You two just found something on this beach. This is where it started." She pointed at a pale, frothy cap of rock along the rim. "Lava fizzes, like a shaken fizzy drink. All that gas got trapped as bubbles, and then the lava cooled and froze the fizz mid-pop. That's pumice. The holes are the bubbles."

Nina held {rock_name} up beside it. Same froth. Same pinprick holes, like the bubbles at the top of a glass of lemonade, only stone.

"And your obsidian?" Ranger Jo pointed to the flow's edge, where the lava had met air and sea. "Cooled so fast it turned to glass. No time for bubbles. No time for anything."

"So the rock tells you," I said slowly, "how the lava behaved."

"The holes, the colour, the weight," said Ranger Jo. "That's the lava's handwriting."

Biscuit barked at the whole volcano, just to be thorough.

Back home, Nina wrote the label for the egg-carton box: {rock_name} — the rock that floats. And it sits on my windowsill still, pale and holey and full of frozen fizz, next to a stone so light it feels like a trick. Because it is one. The lava's best one.

"The museum," said Nina. "I want to test them properly."

The museum room was small and cool and smelled of old wood. A volunteer named Fern brought out a tank of water, and her eyes twinkled. "Drop it in, then."

Nina lowered {rock_name} into the water. It floated. It bobbed gloriously on the surface like the tiniest boat, and Biscuit barked at it so hard his ears flapped.

"Now this," said Fern, and she brought out a piece of obsidian in two careful hands. "Glass, this one. Hold it flat in your palm, like me." She showed us, and we did, and the black stone lay in Nina's hand, heavy as a secret, shining like a dark mirror.

Then Fern slid a big magnifier over the pumice, and we leaned in. The holes swam up huge — hundreds of tiny bubbles, frozen mid-fizz, like the top of a fizzy drink stopped in time. "The lava fizzed," said Fern, "and the gas got trapped as bubbles before it could pop. Light, holey pumice. But lava that cools in a flash has no time for bubbles at all. Heavy, shiny obsidian."

Nina wrote in her notebook, her tongue between her teeth: "The texture, the colour, the weight — that's the lava's own handwriting."

Fern set one more stone beside them with a wink. "This one fell from the sky. Do you think it tells its story the same way?"

But that is another story. On my windowsill, {rock_name} still floats in its egg-carton box, keeping its secrets politely.

gathered_but_unused: Some pumice stones can float on water because they are so full of tiny air holes that they are lighter than the water they push aside.
The holes in a volcanic rock are frozen bubbles: gas was fizzing in the hot lava, and when the lava cooled quickly, the bubbles were locked in place forever.
Obsidian is a natural glass that forms when lava cools so fast that its atoms never get time to stack themselves into crystals.
A sharp flake of obsidian can have an edge thinner than a steel razor blade, which is why people long ago used it for cutting tools.
Two rocks made from the very same lava can feel completely different in your hand — one light and holey, one heavy and glassy — depending only on how the lava cooled and how much gas was in it.
Pumice feels rough and scratchy, almost like a stiff sponge, because it is mostly holes with only thin walls of rock between them.
Lava that oozes slowly, like thick honey, lets gas escape gently, so the rock it makes has few bubbles; lava that froths up violently traps lots of gas and makes holey rock.
Volcanic rocks come in many colours — black, grey, rusty red, even pale cream — and the colour hints at what minerals were in the lava and how much air touched it while it cooled.
